svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. The scope ladder, and the two rungs most people use
svg.desc: Five rungs of permission scope, from most restrictive to least. Deny is the default answer. Ask every time grants access for one use and then expires. While using grants access only while the application is in the foreground. A limited subset grants only the specific photographs or contacts you chose, and is the newest and least used rung. Full or always access grants the entire library or background access and very few applications need it. A band below notes that most people treat permissions as a choice between the first rung and the last, that the middle three are where the useful answers are, and that both platforms now revoke permissions automatically from applications you have stopped opening.
svg.text: Figure 3: The Scope Ladder
Every sensitive permission has five rungs. Most people use the first and the last, and the useful answers are all in the middle.
1. Deny
no access
The correct default, and the one you can afford to be wrong about.
You can grant it later, when something visibly breaks. You cannot un-collect what was already
taken, so the cautious answer costs you an interruption rather than a disclosure.
2. Ask every time
one use, then it lapses
The right rung for anything you use occasionally, and the most under-used option.
Available for location, camera and microphone. The grant lasts that session only, so an
application you open twice a year never accumulates standing access to anything.
3. While using
foreground only
The right answer for the large majority of location grants, and not the one asked for.
Access exists only while the application is open in front of you. A navigation application works
perfectly here. So does a delivery application, which asks for the rung above regardless.
4. A limited subset
only what you picked
The newest rung, the least known, and the one that changes most for photos and contacts.
You choose the items and the application gets those and nothing else. Selecting individual
contacts arrived on iPhone in 2024, and developers complained loudly, which is informative.
5. Full, or always
everything, always
The whole library, the whole address book, or location while the application is closed.
Very few applications genuinely need this, and each one should be a decision you can justify
aloud. The address book is the sharpest case: it is a list of other people, and nobody asked them.
Three things that follow from the ladder

g.text: The prompt is not the ladder. An application asks at the rung it wants. The other rungs live in settings afterwards, which is where most of this work actually happens.
Both platforms now revoke automatically. Permissions lapse on applications you stopped opening. Useful, and a reason to check what got revoked rather than a substitute for looking.
Rung four is where the recent gains are. If you set your permissions two years ago, the limited options you have now did not exist then. Go back and look.

svg.text: One pass down this ladder for every application holding location, photographs, contacts, microphone or camera. It takes about twenty minutes.
And remember Figure 1: this closes one channel of three. It is worth doing, and it is not the whole job.
The application you delete drops off all three at once, which is why the ladder ends where it does.
